segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is also a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the holy ones, and stand by her in whatever matter she may need you, for she herself has been a patron of many, and of me as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my coworkers in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who risked their own necks for my life; not only I but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles give thanks to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet also the assembly in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Asia for Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Mary, who has labored much for you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsfolk and fellow prisoners, who are outstanding among the apostles and who were in Christ before I was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Urbanus, our coworker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Apelles, tested and approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet the beloved Persis, who has labored much in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is mine too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the holy ones with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the assemblies of Christ greet you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I urge you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who create divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you learned, and turn away from them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such people are slaves not to our Lord Christ but to their own belly, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For your obedience has become known to everyone. So I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Timothy, my coworker, greets you, and so do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsfolk.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and so does our brother Quartus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word ordinarily means someone who serves or carries out a task for another, and this translation usually renders it “servant.” Here it is tied to a particular assembly (“of the assembly in Cenchreae”), which suggests a recognized role, so “deacon” is used. Whether Paul means a defined office or simply that Phoebe served that community is disputed, and many translations have “servant.”

The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep; others use “God's people.” The word is applied to all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

Older translations have “helper” or “succorer”; several recent ones have “patron” or “benefactor.” In the period the word and its masculine counterpart were used of a person of means and standing who protected and supported others, so more than general helpfulness is implied. The Greek also plays on a related verb: the Romans are to “stand by” Phoebe because she has stood up for many.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it “Gentiles” in that sense and “nations” where peoples as such are meant; it is one Greek word throughout.

The Greek form could in theory be a woman's name, Junia, or a man's name, Junias, depending on accentuation, which the earliest manuscripts do not mark. Junia was a common Latin woman's name, while Junias as a male name is not securely attested, and early interpreters took the person to be a woman. Most scholars and recent translations now read Junia; she and Andronicus may have been husband and wife.

The phrase can mean that Andronicus and Junia were distinguished members of the group called apostles, or that they were well known to the apostles. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, favor the first reading, which is followed here. A minority argue for the second. If the first is right, “apostles” is used in the wider sense of commissioned emissaries, not the Twelve.

The word means relatives, and Paul uses it in Romans 9:3 for his fellow Jews as a people. Most interpreters think he means fellow Jews here and in verses 11 and 21 rather than members of his own family, but closer kinship cannot be ruled out. “Kinsfolk” and “kinsman” leave both possibilities open.

Most translations have “serve.” The verb is the one related to the ordinary Greek word for a slave, and denotes belonging to and working for a master. The stronger rendering keeps it distinct from the different word-group translated “servant” in this translation.

Letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, and Tertius, who penned this one for Paul, adds his own greeting here. “In the Lord” may go with “greet you,” as rendered, or with “wrote down”; the Greek word order allows either.

The Greek title means a manager or steward, here of the city, most likely Corinth, from which the letter appears to have been sent. It indicates a post in the city's financial administration, but exactly which office, and of what rank, is uncertain. Such a post could be held by a person of high status or by a public slave or freedman.

notes.phrase: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.
notes.note: This verse is absent from several of the earliest manuscripts, and many modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote; it largely repeats the blessing in verse 20. The Greek edition translated here includes it. The same edition does not print the closing doxology that most English Bibles number as verses 25–27, because that passage appears at different places in the manuscripts and is absent from some.

candidates.reason: The plural addressing mixed communities recurs in every letter, and translators divide between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
The verb is cognate with δοῦλος, and whether it is “serve” or “be a slave to” should match the register's slave/servant distinction across the New Testament.
It ranges from blood relative to fellow member of a people, and a reader would be misled if it varied between “relative,” “kinsman” and “fellow Jew” across Luke, John and Romans.
It is very frequent, and translators vary between “urge,” “appeal,” “exhort,” “encourage” and “comfort,” so the senses need to be fixed.
It is Paul's recurring term for his associates across the letters, and translators vary between “fellow worker,” “coworker” and “helper.”
